claims.text: In as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type nanoscale films or nanoribbons, magnetocaloric response and low-field hysteresis are largely governed by heat-transfer efficiency across the film-substrate interface.
Limited film-substrate thermal coupling reduces heat dissipation from the film.
Reduced heat dissipation slows magnetic-domain reorientation and broadens magnetic hysteresis.
Changing substrate thermal conductivity while holding deposition conditions fixed is a controlled intervention for changing film heat transfer.
Changing substrate thermal conductivity will significantly change the film-substrate interfacial thermal resistance.
The relevant FeMnNiGeSi-type films possess a magnetostructural transition near room temperature.
Heat-transfer limitations become critical near the magnetostructural transition when cycle conditions approach the heat-dissipation limit.
Film-substrate interfacial thermal resistance controls heat-transfer rate, local temperature gradients, and magnetic-domain dynamics.
Poor thermal coupling causes heat to accumulate locally during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Local heat accumulation delays thermally driven magnetic-domain reorientation.
Delayed magnetic-domain reorientation enlarges the hysteresis loop.
Improved thermal coupling permits faster heat dissipation.
Improved thermal coupling produces more efficient magnetocaloric switching, a sharper response, and narrower hysteresis.
Films on high-thermal-conductivity substrates will exhibit a larger magnetocaloric temperature change per field cycle than films on low-thermal-conductivity substrates.
Films on high-thermal-conductivity substrates will exhibit narrower magnetic hysteresis than films on low-thermal-conductivity substrates.
Better substrate thermal coupling will increase the maximum useful magnetic-cooling cycle frequency.
The predicted trend applies below approximately 100 Oe near the magnetostructural transition, where heat-transfer limitation is dominant.
Post-deposition treatment may alter microstructure and invalidate the predicted trend.
The relative quantitative contributions of intrinsic magnetic-domain kinetics and thermal coupling remain uncertain and may depend on uncharacterized microstructure.
A lack of statistically significant substrate-dependent differences in magnetocaloric magnitude, hysteresis width, and cycle-frequency limit would falsify the proposed thermal-coupling hypothesis.
